newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin sees progress on EMU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: Jospin sees progress on EMU budget pact.

text.p: France on Thursday edged towards an agreement on a European Union budget discipline pact, saying its concern to redirect European economic policy towards promoting growth and jobs had been understood.

Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said after talks with European Commission President Jacques Santer, who brought proposals for a resolution on coordinating economic and employment policy at next week's Amsterdam EU summit, that they had made progress.

"The preoccupations we are expressing do not simply concern France. They concern the whole of Europe," Jospin told reporters. "Therefore I think these concerns have been understood. We are making progress."
Santer said both he and Jospin wanted to make the Amsterdam summit next Monday and Tuesday a success.

"In that we agree with the aims of the stability pact, if we do not want to change the modalities nor the nature, and if we also agree on the timetable for monetary and economic union, I believe -- with the proposals we made during the Ecofin meeting last Monday -- all elements are on the table to reach an agreement," Santer told reporters after a separate meeting with conservative President Jacques Chirac.
He said his proposals concerned employment and growth but gave no further details.

The new French government threw a spanner into the EU's works on Monday by requesting a delay to study the stability pact, negotiated last December and due to be approved by EU leaders in Amsterdam. It has not yet said whether it will accept it at the summit.
"We very much want the Amsterdam summit to succeed, I think that is also the wish of the prime minister," Santer said.

European Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said he believed the EU would be able to resolve the row by making more explicit reference to the need to coordinate economic policies and fight to reduce unemployment.

He said the solution was to develop provisions for economic policy coordination written into the Maastricht treaty on European union in 1991, which have largely remained a dead letter while the 15-nation bloc, driven by Germany, has focused on fiscal discipline and price stability.
France's new government says it is merely seeking to apply the treaty fully.

EU diplomats said any additional resolution adopted in a goodwill gesture to France could be largely declaratory, with few practical consequences and no obligation to change policy or allow the EU to launch employment initiatives.

Amid intensive efforts to ensure the stability pact is approved in Amsterdam, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Finance Minister Theo Waigel will meet Chirac and Jospin in Poitiers, France, on Friday to prepare for the EU summit.

Both Waigel and French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn have said there could be an emergency meeting of EU economics and finance ministers in Amsterdam on Sunday to draft an overall agreement for the summit.
